title: Harvest and Hymn
premise: Folklorist Vesper Sterling arrives in the drowned-hollow village of Marrowfen to record its harvest hymns, only to discover the villagers refuse to sing any song twice—and that the parish bell, melted down in 1911, has begun ringing again each dusk. As he transcribes the hymns, Vesper realizes they are not songs but instructions: a liturgy that counts the living, refills the old well, and claims a body for every verse sung aloud. When his own family name appears in the oldest verse, Vesper must lead the villagers' children out ahead of the final count, sealing the well by singing the hymn backward alone—an act that costs him his voice, his name in the village records, and nearly his life. The book ends with the village silent and the well dry, while somewhere far away, a new bell begins to ring.
about_author: Lior Voss is the pen name of a former archivist of regional hymnals who spent a decade cataloguing songs no congregation would sing twice. They live near a reservoir and keep, by their own admission, too many doors counted.

chapters.title: The Song They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Vesper Sterling, a folklorist haunted by a childhood of borrowed identities, arrives in Marrowfen to record its harvest hymns. POV: Vesper. He coaxes one verse from an old woman, Edith, who goes pale mid-line and refuses to continue. The emotional beat is uneasy curiosity curdling into dread when she whispers, 'You've already heard it once. That's how it starts.'

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Vesper settles into the rented parsonage, obsessively counting doors and keeping lights burning, a ritual he inherited from a mother he barely remembers. POV: Vesper, with a flashback to his mother's counting. At dusk, a bell tolls—though the church bell was melted down in 1911. The beat: the comfort of ritual fails for the first time, and Vesper realizes his habits came from somewhere that knew Marrowfen.

chapters.title: What Edith Buried
chapters.summary: Vesper presses Edith about the hymn; she shows him a ledger of village births and deaths where names vanish in cycles, including a Sterling line he never knew existed. POV: Vesper. The emotional beat shifts from investigation to vertigo—his identity is not his own but an inheritance, and the ledger's latest entry, freshly inked, bears his name.

chapters.title: The Well Listens
chapters.summary: Following the bell's toll, Vesper descends to the old well at the hollow's edge and hears the missing verses rising from the water in his mother's voice. POV: Vesper, intercut with the well's perspective in second person. The beat is seduction: the well offers him belonging, a family, a name that fits—and he nearly sings back.

chapters.title: Children of the Count
chapters.summary: The village's children begin sleepwalking toward the well at night, humming the hymn in unison. POV: Mara, the schoolteacher, who recruits Vesper. Together they bar the schoolhouse doors. The emotional beat is reluctant alliance—Mara distrusts outsiders, but her terror for the children outweighs it, and Vesper learns he is not the only one keeping count.

chapters.title: The Verse That Names You
chapters.summary: Vesper deciphers the hymn's structure: it is not a song but a census, each verse claiming one soul, and the final verse names the whole Sterling line. POV: Vesper, reading his ancestor's confession hidden in the hymnal's binding. The beat is horror of inheritance—his mother didn't flee Marrowfen; she was sent ahead, a first payment.

chapters.title: Bellringer
chapters.summary: The melted bell rings continuously now, and the village adults, hollow-eyed, begin singing the verses willingly, trading their neighbors' names to postpone their own. POV: Mara, watching the congregation she's known all her life turn. The beat is betrayal and isolation—Marrowfen will not be saved; it must be escaped.

chapters.title: Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: Vesper and Mara gather the children for a night flight out of the hollow, but the roads loop back, and the well's water rises to meet them, carrying faces. POV: alternating Vesper and Mara. The beat is desperate momentum—Vesper realizes the only road out runs through the well itself, and the hymn must be sung backward from inside it.

chapters.title: The Backward Hymn
chapters.summary: At the well's lip, Vesper sings the census in reverse, un-naming the claimed, while the water pulls and the bell cracks. His mother's voice surfaces one last time to help him finish. POV: Vesper. The climax's beat is sacrifice: he gives the well his own name and voice as the final un-counted verse, and the water goes still and low.

chapters.title: A Man With No Name in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Vesper—mute, unnamed in every record—watches the children board a bus out of Marrowfen with Mara, the well dry and the church silent. POV: Vesper, in spare, voiceless prose. The resolution's beat is bittersweet survival: he paid the price of it, and identity, he finally understands, is what you give away, not what you're given. Far off, a new bell begins to ring.
